findings.title: I leaked credentials on purpose for four months. Here's who took them, and what they did next.
findings.summary_md: Lauren Proehl ran a honeypot from July 7 to November 7, 2026, with a walkable git repository, a fake mail server, fake AI inference endpoints, and more than 500 canary AWS keys. Attackers used 155 of those keys from 12,353 distinct IPs; 72 percent of used keys went to SES or SNS send-quota checks and 36 percent touched Bedrock. The report measured a median of 37 minutes from theft to first use and documented a checker that graded stolen AI keys across five providers from 20 residential connections in 14 countries.

findings.title: Three breaches, endless leaks: Your AI supply chain needs canaries
findings.summary_md: Dragos chief research officer HD Moore published the underlying study of nearly two million prompts sent from July through November 2026 with unique URLs, DNS names, and canary AWS credentials through AI routers and inference marketplaces. The report says three hosting providers were compromised, resellers read customer prompts through ordinary request logging, and some requests marked Zero Data Retention were still fetched or forwarded to Chinese labs. Seeded keys were used for tens of thousands of AWS API calls, including S3 listing, Secrets Manager and Parameter Store lookups, Bedrock model enablement, and IAM user creation.

findings.title: HD Moore: We seeded 2m canaries into popular AI services and tracked where they were stolen and abused
findings.summary_md: HD Moore posted the first public summary of the study on Infosec Exchange and linked to the full Dragos report. He said two million canaries were seeded into popular AI services and tracked after they were stolen and abused. The post listed three compromised providers, resellers stealing prompts through built-in logging, and providers ignoring Zero Data Retention and privacy flags.
